entries.name: Sugar kelp
entries.leaves: single undivided blade, no true leaves
entries.voxel_shape: long undulating brown blade on a short perennial stipe with a branching holdfast; underwater only
entries.notes: The kelp of cold high latitudes: dominant on rock in Greenlandic and Norwegian fjords where sea ice leaves a summer open-water window. Mature annual blades average 1-2 m with stipes under 25 cm.

entries.name: Dragon kelp
entries.leaves: huge corrugated blade with a hollow ribbed midrib (fistulae), no true leaves
entries.voxel_shape: canopy kelp: branching holdfast, short stipe, one enormous strap blade 10-25 m long floating toward the surface
entries.notes: The giant of the ice-edge Pacific: forms canopy beds in the Aleutians, up to 25 m documented. Often listed under its synonym Alaria fistulosa.

entries.name: Arctic suction-cup kelp
entries.growth: slow; grows 90% of its new blade in darkness under the ice
entries.leaves: broad ovate blade divided by annual constrictions
entries.voxel_shape: small stout brown kelp: flat lanceolate blade on a short solid stipe, discoidal holdfast
entries.notes: An Arctic endemic engineered for long polar night: it spends its stored carbon on a new blade while still under an 8-month turbid ice canopy (the Boulder Patch off Prudhoe Bay is the classic site).

entries.name: Sieve kelp
entries.leaves: leathery brown blade pierced by regular oval holes
entries.voxel_shape: stiff corrugated blade with regularly spaced holes, single stout stipe, claw-like holdfast
entries.notes: The unpierced look is wrong: the holes are the point. Dominant or co-dominant in Canadian Arctic ice-scapes (eastern Arctic surveys average ~15% benthic cover).

entries.name: Dabberlocks
entries.leaves: single wavy blade with a short midrib and sporophylls at its base
entries.voxel_shape: slender wavy blade keeled by a short midrib, forked stipe with a dense holdfast
entries.notes: A familiar edible of cold Atlantic shores; frequent in Greenlandic and Icelandic kelp belts. Winged kelp with a midrib that splits into the blade, unlike Saccharina.

entries.name: Oarweed
entries.leaves: glossy blade splitting into strap-like fingers
entries.voxel_shape: hand-like frond: several broad strap lobes from one smooth flexible stipe, discoidal holdfast
entries.notes: Classic exposed-shore kelp of the NE Atlantic, reaching its northern limit around the Arctic Circle. Finger-split blade separates it from the undivided Saccharina.

entries.name: Long-stipe sugar kelp
entries.leaves: single broad blade on a long hollow stipe (1-2 m)
entries.voxel_shape: sugar kelp stretched tall: same undivided blade but on a very long flexible stipe
entries.notes: The NW Atlantic sibling of sugar kelp, dominant along the Greenland gradient where ice-free days decide how deep kelp grows. Often confused with S. latissima further south.

entries.name: Eelgrass
entries.leaves: long ribbon-like leaves from a creeping rhizome; true leaves and true flowers
entries.voxel_shape: underwater meadow of flat green ribbons on a sandy or muddy bed, swaying in one direction
entries.notes: The only seagrass reaching the Arctic Circle (to ~70°N in Norway and Greenland), surviving 7-month ice cover. Meadows are clonal and can persist for centuries; growth optimum is warmer water, so Arctic beds are slow.

entries.name: Two-rockweed
entries.leaves: flat olive-brown fronds with a forked tip and no midrib
entries.voxel_shape: forked intertidal rockweed tuft clinging to the wave-washed splash zone
entries.notes: The Arctic shore's brown belt: intertidal rocks encrusted with low forked rockweed, often the most visible plant of an ice-free Arctic shore.

entries.name: Knotted wrack
entries.growth: very slow perennial, can live many decades
entries.leaves: long olive fronds with regularly spaced single air bladders
entries.voxel_shape: long olive chains of pea-sized bladders hanging from sheltered intertidal rocks
entries.notes: Reaches only its subarctic fringe in frozen-ocean waters. Where it grows it dominates sheltered shores; individual fronds age like shrubs.

entries.name: Whip Chordaria
entries.leaves: unbranched cylindrical olive cords, whip-like
entries.voxel_shape: limp dark green whips anchored to stones in shallow cold water
entries.notes: A plain-looking cold-water brown alga, common in belts of fine sand and rock where ice scours out other species.

entries.name: Arctic green hair
entries.leaves: tufted dark green branched filaments
entries.voxel_shape: low dark-green woolly tuft clinging to intertidal stones and kelp holdfasts
entries.notes: The untidy green fringe under every Arctic rockweed: filamentous tufts of the high intertidal and the littoral fringe.

entries.name: Dulse
entries.leaves: flat reddish-purple lobed blades, no midrib
entries.voxel_shape: small purple-red hand-shaped blades epiphytic on kelp stipes or on rock
uses: food (dried snack, high protein and minerals)
entries.notes: The cold-water nori: eaten dried for centuries on Atlantic coasts. In the Arctic it grows as an understory on Laminaria and rock.

entries.name: Giant Antarctic kelp
entries.growth: seasonal burst after ice break-out, slow rest of year
entries.leaves: enormous strap-like brown lamina, no true leaves
entries.voxel_shape: the only near-giant of Antarctic waters: vast leathery straps rising 10+ m from 15-40 m depth
uses: major benthic producer under the ice
entries.notes: Not a true kelp (Desmarestiales, not Laminariales) and the largest brown alga in the Southern Ocean: Antarctica has no laminarian kelps at all. Dominates sublittoral rock 15-40 m under the ice.

entries.name: Sulphur-acid Desmarestia
entries.leaves: bushy forked brown branches
entries.voxel_shape: dense brown bushy thicket 5-20 m deep in the sublittoral
entries.notes: Desmarestia cells hold sulfuric acid in vacuoles (pH near 1), a chemical fence against grazers; the tissue turns mushy if brought onto land. Co-dominant with Ascoseira on King George Island platforms.

entries.name: Forked Desmarestia
entries.leaves: flat opposite-branched brown fronds with acid vacuoles
entries.voxel_shape: dark forked fronds 10-30 m deep, deeper-water sibling of D. menziesii
entries.notes: The deeper-water counterpart: dominates below 15 m where H. grandifolius and D. menziesii thin out. Height not well quantified in the literature; treat as large (1-4 m).

entries.name: Wonderful Ascoseira
entries.leaves: strap-like olive lamina, fucalean life history
entries.voxel_shape: single leathery strap rising from the shallow platform, 2-15 m deep
entries.notes: The lone genus of its order: an Antarctic fucoid with a kelp's body and a wrack's life cycle. Endemic to the Peninsula and South Shetlands.

entries.name: Austral dulse
entries.growth: seasonal anticipator, new blades in August
entries.leaves: unbranched reddish-purple glossy blades up to 70 cm
entries.voxel_shape: low red-purple straps in dense intertidal and upper-subtidal belts
uses: Antarctic analogue of dulse, eaten fresh or dried
entries.notes: Dominant intertidal red alga of the Peninsula; confirmed alive at 100 m depth, the deepest in-situ macroalga yet recorded there. Pre-grows its blades in winter darkness.

entries.name: Antarctic bladderweed
entries.leaves: yellowish-brown bladder-topped stalks
entries.voxel_shape: tiny bladder-tipped bladders of the intertidal and the splash zone
entries.notes: Ubiquitous little alga of the Peninsula intertidal: thin stalks tipped by yellowish gas bladders, one of the first colonists when sea ice retreats.

entries.name: Antarctic laver
entries.leaves: thin translucent sheet, one cell thick
entries.voxel_shape: emerald tissue-paper sheets draped on rocks at low tide
entries.notes: A one-cell-thick green sheet eaten in the southern ocean islands; the Antarctic answer to nori.

entries.name: Wrinkled Prasiola
entries.growth: very fast, responds to nitrogen within days
entries.leaves: small crumpled dark-green rosettes
entries.voxel_shape: greasy dark-green rosettes carpeting splash-zone rock near penguin rookeries
entries.notes: Fertilized by penguin guano: Prasiola carpets explode within days of guano deposition, one of the fastest responses of any Antarctic plant to nitrogen.

entries.name: Arctic ice diatom
entries.growth: fast at ice break-up, colonial chains
entries.voxel_shape: brown curtains of diatom chains dangling 10 cm-3 m under multi-year ice; strands exceeding 8 m reported
uses: base of the ice-edge food web
keystone feed for amphipods and krill
entries.notes: The ice's own harvest: hangs in mucilage-glued chains from multi-year sea ice, contributing up to ~45% of Arctic primary production in low-ice years. When the ice melts the mats sink and feed the benthos. Render as translucent brown under-ice curtains, never as solid blocks.

entries.name: Frost Nitzschia
entries.growth: fast in first-year ice brine channels
entries.voxel_shape: invisible at game scale; a golden-brown smear in brine channels of first-year ice
entries.notes: Microscopic pennate diatom; the standard of the first-year ice understory. Lives at brine temperatures far below 0°C. If ever modeled, it is a particle effect or a water-column tint, not an entity.

entries.name: Bipolar ice diatom
entries.growth: fast in ice interior and brine pockets
entries.voxel_shape: invisible at game scale; bipolar sea-ice specialist of brine inclusions
uses: model organism for polar algal adaptation
entries.notes: Lives in both poles' sea ice; sequenced genomes show how it freezes itself gracefully. Microscopic chain-forming diatom of the ice interior.

entries.name: Antarctic ice diatom
entries.voxel_shape: invisible at game scale; cocoa-tinted bloom films under Antarctic fast ice
uses: base of the Antarctic ice-edge food web
entries.notes: Co-dominant with F. cylindrus in Antarctic sea ice; the paired Fragilariopsis species underwrite the whole Southern Ocean ice harvest.

entries.name: Ross Sea ice diatom
entries.growth: fast, forms long strands under landfast ice
entries.voxel_shape: sparse but long pale strands beneath landfast ice
entries.notes: The Antarctic counterpart to Melosira: long-stranded sub-ice diatom, mainly under landfast ice near the coast. Strands of several metres have been reported late in the Antarctic spring.

entries.name: Frost dinoflagellate
entries.voxel_shape: invisible at game scale; red-brown cysts latent in sea ice
entries.notes: A genuinely cold-loving dinoflagellate isolated from Antarctic sea ice; its genome exists precisely because polar biology is strange. Microscopic.

entries.name: Arctic Phaeocystis
entries.voxel_shape: invisible colonies globules of mm-cm mucus; water looks soupy and fish-oily near a bloom
uses: major DMS source, feeds cloud formation
entries.notes: A haptophyte living in gelatinous globules; its DMS emissions seed polar cloud condensation nuclei. Blooms in Arctic and sub-Arctic waters when light returns.

entries.name: Antarctic Phaeocystis
entries.voxel_shape: invisible colonies; turns the ice margin jade-green during the bloom
uses: engine of the Ross Sea bloom
dominant DMS source in the Southern Ocean
entries.notes: Dominant phytoplankton of the Ross Sea; in low-iron years it yields to diatoms, but when it wins it runs the whole bloom and the local climate chemistry with it.

entries.name: Ice-edge Thalassiosira
entries.voxel_shape: invisible at game scale; centric diatom chains at the melt front
entries.notes: A round-valved centric diatom tied to the advancing melt front; the first thing to bloom when the ice opens in spring.

entries.name: Social Chaetoceros
entries.voxel_shape: invisible at game scale; spiny chains that clog fine nets
entries.notes: Hedgehog-like setae make it one of the easiest diatoms to know by net sample; a standard spring-bloomer in sub-polar fjords.

entries.name: Norwegian Dinophysis
entries.voxel_shape: invisible at game scale; red-tides of armored dinoflagellates
entries.notes: Cold-fjord dinoflagellate behind diarrhetic shellfish poisoning events in western Norway; the reason Arctic shellfish have harvest windows.

entries.name: Psychrophilic Mrakia yeast
entries.growth: very slow; optimal near 10°C, cannot grow past ~18°C
entries.voxel_shape: invisible at game scale; a bright orange-pink smear on rotten Antarctic snow and sea sediments
entries.notes: An obligate psychrophile yeast, first isolated from Antarctic snow and sea sediments; one of the better genomic models for life below freezing.

entries.name: Antarctic hair grass
entries.leaves: wiry dark-green blades in small tussocks
entries.voxel_shape: wiry green tussocks on ice-free coastal ledges and moss carpets, seaward of the frozen ocean
uses: One of only two Antarctic flowering plants
entries.notes: Grows on the ice-free coastal fringe above the Antarctic frozen ocean (Peninsula and South Shetlands), never underwater. Place only on shore columns bordering the biome.

entries.name: Antarctic pearlwort
entries.growth: slow cushion, widest on dry warm slopes
entries.leaves: small bright-green awl leaves in dense cushions
entries.voxel_shape: dense bright-green star cushions on dry north-facing coastal rubble
uses: One of only two Antarctic flowering plants
entries.notes: The other Antarctic phanerogam: tiny cushions on dry, north-facing coastal rock beside the frozen ocean. Like D. antarctica, strictly a shore-fringe plant for this biome.
